title: A verse alone (Genesis 1:1)
hook: read Bereshit bara Elohim in Hebrew, by yourself

segments.voice: Yesterday, everyday Hebrew: mazal tov, b'ezrat Hashem, l'chaim, and todah, from the root of Judah's name. Your line was todah. Who heard it from you? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

A single line of Hebrew, black letters, no English underneath. For a long stretch now, this path has been handing you pieces: the shapes of letters, the sounds they make, the roots that hide inside words. Somebody else always did the reading. Today the roles switch. Here is the line the Torah scroll begins with: Bereshit bara Elohim et hashamayim ve'et ha'aretz. In the King James words, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Today you take it apart yourself, word by word, and put it back together.
screen: `ONE LINE, NO ENGLISH.` → `THE ROLES SWITCH.` → `BERESHIT BARA ELOHIM.`

segments.voice: A verse alone. Go slowly. First, bereshit. The opening letter, bet, is a little word glued on the front: in. Then reshit, beginning. Some readers hear rosh inside it, the word for head, as in Rosh Hashanah, the head of the year. In the beginning, at the head of things. Second, bara, created. Look at its letters: bet, resh, alef. Now look back at bereshit. Bet, resh, alef are its first three letters too. The verb is hiding inside the first word, before you even reach it. Elohim follows: God. Third, a word English can't translate at all: et. It's spelled alef, tav, the first letter of the alphabet and the last. In Hebrew grammar it simply points ahead to the thing being acted on. But some readers have seen more in it: the whole alphabet, beginning to end, standing at the start of the world. Fourth, the pair at the end. Hashamayim, the heavens; ha is the. Ve'et ha'aretz, and the earth; ve is and, and there's et again, pointing at the earth too. Heavens and earth: everything above, everything below. Now put it back together. Bereshit bara Elohim et hashamayim ve'et ha'aretz. You have just read, in the language it was written in, the opening line of the Torah, one word at a time. That's what a verse alone means: a line short enough to hold in one breath. Bereshit bara.
screen: `BERESHIT: IN THE BEGINNING.` · `BARA HIDES INSIDE BERESHIT.` · `ET: ALEF TO TAV.` · `THE HEAVENS AND THE EARTH.` · then, large: `BERESHIT BARA ELOHIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read it slowly. Settle, and breathe. Say the first word on an out-breath: bereshit. Pause. On the next breath, bara. Then Elohim. Then et. Then hashamayim. Then ve'et ha'aretz. Don't rush to the meaning; let each word take a whole breath. Then go back and say the whole verse, once, at your own pace. If you stumble, start again; there's no audience. If you pray, you can let the verse itself be your words, the way it opens the Torah each year. Otherwise, let the last two words stay with you: the heavens, and the earth you're sitting on. The bell holds the time.
screen: `ONE WORD, ONE BREATH.` · `THEN THE WHOLE VERSE.` · `THE HEAVENS, AND THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: A verse alone. Genesis one, verse one, read by yourself in Hebrew: bereshit bara Elohim et hashamayim ve'et ha'aretz. In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. Today's word.

Your line: bereshit bara. Today, at the start of one thing, a meal, a task, a conversation, say those two words under your breath. Tomorrow, the close of the whole year. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Genesis 1:1 opens the Torah and is read aloud in synagogue each year when the reading cycle begins again after Simchat Torah; some Jewish learners practice reading Hebrew on verses like this one, word by word.

bet, resh, alef: the verb hides inside the first word.
et is alef and tav. it points to the thing acted on, and English has no word for it. ve means and.

fork.setup: you're reading Genesis 1:1 in Hebrew and reach et, alef and tav, a word English skips. what do some readers see in it?
options: a scribe's mistake to be ignored.
the whole alphabet, first letter to last.
fork.reveal: grammar says et points to the object, but some readers see the whole alef-bet, alef to tav, standing at the start of the world.

original.note: Hebrew: in the beginning God created; the opening words of Genesis 1:1.

trapdoor: what you thought: in the beginning God created, a sentence you already know in English.
what it means: bereshit bara Elohim, where bara's letters already sit inside bereshit, and et, alef to tav, points at the heavens and the earth.
what a scholar hears: Rashi argued that bereshit is grammatically 'in the beginning of', so the verse may open a longer sentence: when God began to create.

sources.quoted: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.

notes: Hebrew of Genesis 1:1 given in transliteration and (partly) in pointed script in the original game. Confirm pointing and pronunciation.
'you can hear rosh inside it': reshit is generally linked to rosh (head); stated as something audible rather than as an etymology. Confirm.
Et (alef-tav) as the direct-object marker; 'some readers' (midrashic and kabbalistic) see the whole alphabet in it. Confirm the framing.
'the line the Torah scroll begins with' is hedged; customs vary (some schools begin with Leviticus). Confirm or soften further.
Trapdoor paraphrases Rashi's grammatical reading of bereshit as construct ('in the beginning of'). Confirm.
